newsitem.title: USA: View of weak European monetary pact fuels dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: View of weak European monetary pact fuels dollar rise.

text.p: The dollar rose on Thursday against most currencies, bolstered by optimism that ongoing negotiations in Dublin over a proposed European monetary pact will end in favour of the U.S. currency.
However, the dollar closed below its session high versus the German mark, dragged lower by a sharp retreat in U.S. stocks for a second consecutive day.
The German-led stability pact is intended to detail the fiscal discipline required among nations seeking to participate in Europe's proposed single currency, the euro.
The German government is determined to ensure that the economic framework for the euro is strict enough to produce a single European currency that is as robust as the mark.

Currency analysts said market-makers bought dollars in order to benefit from the likelihood of a relatively weak or ineffective stability pact, which would put the mark under pressure against the dollar and other European currencies.

"I think there have been enough comments to influence the sentiment that not a great amount will be achieved. The market has become pessimistic," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A.
European negotiators in Dublin expressing doubt over the chances of the stability pact moulded market opinion as several officials warned against premature optimism.
"According to our latest information, one should be careful with such expectations," said Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
The talks precede a two-day summit of European leaders starting Friday that has grabbed the currency market's focus and spurred much speculation over the liklihood of European monetary union.

"I think the market was so optimistic last week with everyone saying monetary union was definitely going to happen and this week the sentiment is not so great," said Greg Perman, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale de France.
The dollar also received support from European Monetary Institute President Alexandre Lamfalussy, who said the dollar was undervalued against European currencies.
An unexpected drop in U.S. November retail sales, falling 0.4 percent against an consensus forecast of a 0.3 percent gain, also helped fuel the dollar's rise.

But by late in the trading day, U.S. Treasuries had erased almost all of their gains and the Dow Jones industrial average ended down nearly 100 points after an initial 30-point gain. The dollar followed suit and pared its gains against most European currencies.

The dollar closed at 1.5410 marks, compared with 1.5379 at Wednesday's close. The dollar also slipped from its session peak against the yen, but still ended higher at 113.15 yen, versus 112.97 at Wednesday's close.

The dollar fell sharply in Asian trade against the yen, but a bout of Australian dollar buying and yen selling brought the slide to a halt. Heavy buying by a U.S. money fund also aided the dollar's recovery against the yen, dealers said.
The market was little moved by tame November U.S. consumer price data. The price index rose 0.3 percent, as expected.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.3105 Swiss francs from 1.3095 at Wednesday's close and fell to Canadian $1.3587 from C$1.3603. Sterling rose to $1.6575 from $1.6532.
